course.title: AP Precalculus
course.description: Build the function toolkit that calculus depends on: how quantities change together, polynomial and rational functions, exponential and logarithmic models, and trigonometric and polar functions.
course.previewDescription: Study how outputs change with inputs, then use polynomial, rational, exponential, logarithmic, and trigonometric functions to describe patterns and build models.

unit.title: Polynomial and Rational Functions
unit.description: See how outputs change with inputs, then use rates of change, zeros, end behavior, asymptotes, and holes to describe polynomial and rational functions and build models from them.

topic.title: Rational Functions and End Behavior
topic.summary: What a rational function is, and how comparing leading terms gives horizontal and slant asymptotes.

lesson.title: Rational Functions and End Behavior
lesson.summary: What a rational function is, and how comparing leading terms gives horizontal and slant asymptotes.
learningGoals: Identify a rational function and recognize where its denominator can make it undefined.
Use the degrees and leading coefficients of the numerator and denominator to find horizontal asymptotes.
Recognize when a rational function has a slant asymptote and describe the end behavior in limit notation.
lesson.bigIdea: For large inputs, a rational function behaves like the quotient of its leading terms. Comparing the sizes of the numerator and denominator tells you whether the outputs settle near a number, follow a line, or grow without bound.
lesson.context: Polynomial end behavior came from one leading term. A rational function has two polynomials fighting for control, so the question becomes which one grows faster, or whether they grow at the same pace.

sections.title: A rational function is a quotient of two polynomials.

blocks.text: A rational function can be written r(x) = p(x)/q(x), where p and q are polynomials and q is not the zero polynomial. At each input, the output measures the size of the numerator relative to the size of the denominator. The function is undefined wherever q(x) = 0.

blocks.caption: Comparing the degrees of numerator and denominator

sections.takeaway: A rational function is a polynomial divided by a polynomial, and it is undefined where the denominator is zero.

sections.title: End behavior comes from comparing the leading terms.

blocks.text: When |x| is large, a polynomial acts like its leading term. So a rational function acts like the quotient of the leading term of the numerator and the leading term of the denominator. What that quotient does depends on which degree is larger.

blocks.caption: End behavior of a rational function from the degrees
rows: A constant: the ratio of leading coefficients
Follows the end behavior of a polynomial; a slant asymptote if the numerator degree is exactly one more

blocks.text: For r(x) = (4x − 1)/(x² + 3), the denominator dominates, so the outputs shrink toward 0. For r(x) = (3x² + 1)/(x² − 5), the degrees are equal and the leading terms give 3x²/x² = 3.

sections.takeaway: Compare degrees first. Equal degrees give a horizontal asymptote at the ratio of the leading coefficients.

sections.title: A horizontal asymptote describes the outputs at the ends.

blocks.text: A horizontal asymptote at y = b means that lim x→∞ r(x) = b, or lim x→−∞ r(x) = b, or both. The outputs get as close to b as you like, though they may not ever equal b at the far ends. For r(x) = (3x² + 1)/(x² − 5), the table shows the outputs closing in on 3.

blocks.title: An asymptote describes the ends only
blocks.text: A graph may cross a horizontal asymptote in the middle. The function r(x) = x/(x² + 1) has the horizontal asymptote y = 0 at both ends, yet r(0) = 0, so the graph meets that line at the origin.

sections.takeaway: A horizontal asymptote is a statement about the far ends, written with limit notation.

sections.title: When the numerator's degree is one greater, the graph follows a slanted line.

blocks.text: Take r(x) = (2x³ − x)/(x² + 1). The numerator has degree 3 and the denominator has degree 2, so the outputs grow without bound. Dividing gives the equivalent form r(x) = 2x − 3x/(x² + 1). The last term shrinks toward 0 for large |x|, so r(x) behaves more and more like 2x.

blocks.caption: Comparing r(x) = (2x³ − x)/(x² + 1) with the line y = 2x

blocks.text: The line y = 2x is a slant asymptote. Topic 1.11 shows how to find the equivalent form using polynomial long division. If the numerator's degree exceeds the denominator's by 2 or more, the outputs still grow without bound, but they follow a curve rather than a line.

sections.takeaway: A numerator degree exactly one greater gives a slant asymptote, found from the quotient of a division.

vocabulary.definition: A function that can be written as a quotient of two polynomials, with a denominator that is not the zero polynomial.
A line that a graph gets closer and closer to, described by what the function does as an input or output grows without bound.
A line y = b that the outputs approach as the input increases or decreases without bound.
A non-horizontal line that the graph of a rational function approaches as the input increases or decreases without bound.

connections.title: Same dominance, new setting
connections.body: Topic 1.6 showed that a polynomial behaves like its leading term at the ends. Here two leading terms compete, and the winner, or the tie, determines the asymptote.
connections.transferQuestion: Why does a larger denominator degree pull the outputs toward 0?
connections.feedback: The denominator grows faster than the numerator, so the ratio shrinks toward 0.

links.label: Review how the leading term dominates

connections.title: Asymptotes meet zeros and holes
connections.body: Topic 1.8 finds where rational functions cross the x-axis. Topic 1.9 finds the vertical asymptotes that appear when the denominator is zero, and Topic 1.10 finds the holes that appear when a factor cancels.
connections.transferQuestion: Where would you look in a rational function for inputs where something unusual happens besides the ends?
connections.feedback: A strong answer says to factor the numerator and denominator and look at where each equals zero.

glossary.definition: The term of a polynomial with the highest power of x.
The coefficient of the leading term of a polynomial.
The behavior of a function's outputs as the input increases without bound or decreases without bound.
Growing larger than any fixed number, or more negative than any fixed number, as the input moves in one direction.
Notation such as lim x→∞ f(x) = ∞ that records what the outputs of a function do as the input grows without bound or approaches a value.
